Judgment

1. This is a complaint instituted under Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (hereinafter referred to as 'PFA Act') for violation of section 2(ia)(a)(b)(m) and section 7 punishable under section 16 of PFA Act.

2. Brief facts leading to filing of the present complaint are that on 05.11.2010 at about 11.30 am,
Food Inspector Sh. V.P.S. Chaudhary, purchased a sample of Coconut Laddoo, a food article, for analysis from Sh. Jagjit Singh, M/s. Jagjit Halwai, Shop No. 4, Behind Hanuman Mandir, Seva Nagar, New Delhi-110003, where the said food article was found stored for sale for human consumption and whereas Sh. Jagjit Singh was found vending of the said food article at the time of taking the sample.
That the sample consisted of 1500 gm. of Coconut Laddoo taken from open tray bearing no declaration.
That the same was taken under the supervision of Sh. P.R. Jha, SDM/LHA.
That the sample was taken after proper mixing with the help of clean and dry spoon in clean and dry tray.
That the said food articles was divided into three equal parts then and there by putting in three clean and dry glass bottles and 40 drops of formalin was added in each counter part of sample.
That each bottle containing the sample was separately packed, fastened and sealed according to the PFA Act, 1954 and Rules 1955.
That the vendor's signatures were obtained on the LHA slip and wrapper of the bottles containing the sample.
That notice in Form VI was given to Sh. Jagjit Singh and the price of sample was also paid to him vide vendor receipt dated 05.11.2010.
That Panchnama too was prepared at the spot and all the documents prepared by Food Inspector were signed by Sh. Jagjit Singh and by the other witness Sh. Shivji Mahto, F.A.

That before starting the sample proceedings,
efforts were made to get the public witnesses to join the proceedings but none came forward, as such Sh. Shivji Mahto, F.A. was joined as witness.

That one part of the sample bearing LHA code No.
71/LHA/30123 along-with copy of memo VII and another copy of memo VII separately in intact condition were sent to Public Analyst and two remaining counterparts of the sample along-with two copies of memo VII were deposited with SDM/LHA in intact conditions.
That all copies of memo VII were bearing the the seal impression of the seal by which the sample was sealed.
That the Public Analyst analysed the sample and found the sample to be adulterated.

The Public Analyst had given his report vide report No. PFA/Enf/3232/2010 dated 20.11.2010 wherein he opined, "The sample is adulterated because it contains added vegetable oil which is not declared as ingredient."
3.

It is further averred that Sh. Jagjit Singh was the vendor cum proprietor of M/s. Jagjit Halwai,
Shop No. 4, Behind Hanuman Mandir, Sewa Nagar, New Delhi-111003 at the time of taking sample and as such he is in-charge of and responsible for day to day conduct of the business of the said shop and responsible for complying with the provisions of the PFA Act 1954 and the Rules made thereunder.

It is alleged that he has violated the provisions of Section 7 of the PFA Act, 1954 read with Section 2(ia) (a), (b) & (m) of PFA Act, 1954 which is punishable under section 16(1)(a) of the PFA Act, 1954.

Upon filing of the present complaint, cognizance was taken vide order dated 23.03.2021.

Upon service of summons, appearance was entered by accused and after complying with the provision under section 207 Cr.P.C, vide order dated 09.06.2011, notice for the offences under section 2(ia)(a)(b)&(m) punishable under section 16(1)(a) read with section 7 of PFA Act was served upon the accused to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
Thereafter, the case was fixed for prosecution evidence.

5. The prosecution examined Sh V.P.S Chaudhary, Food Inspector as PW-1 who deposed that on 005.11.2010, he had visited the shop of the accused where accused Jagjit Singh was found conducting the business of sale of 'Coconut Laddoo'.

That after disclosing his identity, he purchased 1500 grams of coconut Laddoo from an open aluminum tub having no label declaration, after properly mixing with the help of clean and dry spoon in a clean and dry tray.
As per PW-1 he paid Rs.150/- vide vendors receipt Ex.PW1/A as sample price.
That after lifting of sample, it was divided into three parts as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules and separately packed and sealed in clean and dry glass bottles.
That vendor signatures were obtained on the LHA slip.
That thereafter, one counter part of the sample was deposited with the public analyst (PA) on 06.11.2010 and remaining two counterparts were deposited with the LHA.

PW-1 further deposed that on receipt of the PA report Ex PW1/H the sample was found to be adulterarted, thereafter he sent a letter ExPW1/H to STO Ward No. 99 to disclose the constitution of M/s Jagjit Halwai shop.
That as per reply received, no such firm of the accused was found registered with the Sales Tax.
PW-1 further deposed that after obtaining due sanction of the Director, PFA the present complaint was filed against the accused person.

9. In compliance of the directions of Ld. Sessions Court, the statement of the accused under section 313 Cr.P.C was recorded afresh on 09.01.2024.
Thereafter, the accused led defence evidence.

10. The accused examined Sh. S.M Bhardwaj, Public Analyst as DW1 who deposed that he conducted analysis of the food sample 'Coconut Ladoo' from 09.11.2010 to 11.11.2010 and prepared the report on 20.11.2010 Ex.PW1/H.
That as per his report, the sample was found adulterated as it was containing added vegetable oil which was not declared as an ingredient.
That he has received the sample loose in a sealed sample bottle without the original label.
He deposed in cases of loose sample, there are no original labels and thus it was not received.

That in order to conduct test on the loose sample, he relied upon the ingredient disclosed in the Form No.
VI, wherein the ingredients are stated by the FBO himself.
That he received the Form No. VI along with sample for analysis.
He clarified that he has received Form VII not Form VI.
That Form VII was not available on judicial record, however, there was a description of Form VII in para No. 1 page 2 at point A in complaint.
That he could not tell whether Form VII was in Hindi or in English.
That it was the duty of Food Safety Officer to fill up Form VII.
That he did not remember the ingredients which were mentioned in the Form No. VII due to the lapse of time.
That he did not have the Form No. VII available with him.

That as per his report "Added vegetable oil" was found, which was not declared as ingredient because BR of the extracted facts exceeds the prescribed maximum limit of Coconut oil ie 35.5, which clearly shows that some vegetable oil has been added in the sample.
That he has prepared the report after analyzing the list of ingredients as mentioned in Form No. VII.
That FSO mentioned the ingredients as disclosed by the FBO in Form No. VI.
That the sample of this case was of proprietary food.
And standard of proprietary food has not been defined in the PFA Act, 1954.

I heard the submissions of both the sides and perused the record.
12. There is no dispute that the food article in question was a proprietary food.
The proprietary food has been defined under Rule 37A of Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955 (hereinafter referred to as 'PFA Rules') to be one which is not standardized under the PFA Rules.

Rule 37A reads as under:
"37-A. Manufacture of proprietary foods and infant foods: (1) An article of infant milk substitutes/ infant foods whose standards are not prescribed in Appendix 'B' shall be manufactured for sale, exhibited for sale or stored for sale only after obtaining the approval of such article of food and its label from Government of India.
(2) In case of proprietary foods the name of the food or category under which it falls in these rules shall be mentioned on the label

Explanation :- For the purpose of this rule :
(a) and (aa) (infant food & infant) ..... Omitted (b) "Proprietary food", means a food which has not been standardised under the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955."

13. The case of the prosecution is that the accused being the FBO and in-charge of the business added vegetable oil in the preparation of Coconut Ladoo, a proprietary food article, despite the fact that the same was not a declared ingredient.
There are certain key aspects of the case which are important to discuss.
First of all, the Public Analyst declared in its report that the sample was containing vegetable oil which was not declared by the accused.
The Public Analyst was examined as DW1 who deposed that he received form VI along-with the sample wherein the ingredients mentioned by the FBO.
He then corrected himself and again deposed that he received form VII and that the ingredients are mentioned by Food Inspector on the said form.

It is relevant to refer to the prescribed proforma of form VII which is as under:
FORM VII (See Rule 17) Memorandum to public Analyst From ............................
............................
To The Public Analyst, ...................................
....................................
No. Dated..........

The sample described below is sent herewith for analysis under clause (b) of sub-section (1) of Section 10 and/or clause (c) of subsection (1) and Section 11 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.

1. Code number and serial No. of Local Health Authority..............

5
2 . Omitted
4 . Nature of article submitted for analysis.............................................

5. Nature and quantity of preservative, if any, added to the sample......
A copy of this memo, and specimen impression of the seal used to seal the packet of sample is being sent separately by post/hand.
Food Inspector.

This court fails to understand as to how the Public Analyst has declared law on its own that Food Inspector is required to mention ingredients on the form VII when there is no such statutory requirement.
It is further relevant to mention that Form VII has not been produced by the prosecution so that its contents could have been examined by the Court.
The prosecution has failed to explain as to how the Public Analyst has come to a conclusion that the vegetable oil was a non-declared ingredient.
The fact that the Public Analyst has admitted that ingredients were mentioned on the Form VII by the Food Inspector raises suspicion on the report of the Public Analyst.
15. Further, the report of the Public Analyst no where mentions that that the methods by which the sample was got tested was approved by the Govt. as required by section 23 of PFA Act.
Sections 23(1A) (ee) and (hh) of PFA.

The provisions read as under:
"23. Power of the Central Government to make rules.--
(1) The Central Government may, after consultation with the Committee and after previous publication by notification in the Official Gazette, make rules to carry out the provisions of this Act:
..........

(1A) In particular and without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing power,
such rules may provide for all or any of the following matters, namely:--
..........
(ee) defining the laboratories where samples of articles of food or adulterants may be analysed by public analysts under this Act, ..........

Vide notification of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare dated 25.03.2008, under section Section 23 of the 1954 Act, the Central Government has incorporated Rule 4(9) in the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955, which read as under:
"The manuals of method of analysis brought out by Ministry of Health and Family Welfare shall be adopted for analysing the samples of food articles.

sentences.text: 17. In Pepsico India(supra), the Hon'ble Apex Court considered the issue.

The Hon'ble Apex Court while deciding the case, formulated the following questions for consideration:
"(1) In the absence of any prescribed and validated method of analysis under Section 23(1-A)(hh) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, hereinafter referred to as "the 1954 Act", could a prosecution have been launched against the Appellants based on a report submitted by the Public Analyst using the method of the Directorate General of Health Services (D.G.H.S.)?
(2) Could a prosecution have been launched against the Appellants in the absence of any validated method of analysis to ascertain the percentage of pesticide residue present in a Carbonated beverage, which renders the report of the Public Analyst unreliable, particularly when it does not indicate that such percentage of the pesticide residue is injurious to health and, therefore, adulterated within the meaning of Section 2(ia)
(h) of the aforesaid Act?

(3) What is the effect of non-specification of the level of tolerance in respect of the presence of pesticide residue in Sweetened Carbonated Water in the Table appended to Rule 65(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955, hereinafter referred to as "the 1955 Rules"? and (4) What is the liability of the Directors of a company which is said to have committed defaults within the meaning of Section 17 of the 1954 Act, in the light of the decision of this Court in S.M.S. Pharmaceuticals Ltd. Vs. Neeta Bhalla & Anr. [2005 (8) sec 89], when they were neither in charge of nor responsible Da vs Jagjit Singh on 20 August, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/109557362/

sentences.text:
The relevant observations of Hon'ble Supreme Court are as under:
"34.

As far as Grounds 1 and 2 are concerned, the High Court was not convinced with the submission made on behalf of the appellants that in the absence of any prescribed and validated method of analysis under Section 23(1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the 1954 Act,
the report of the Public Analyst, who had used the DGHS method, could not be relied upon, especially when even the Laboratories, where the test for detection of insecticides and pesticides in an article of food could be undertaken, had not been specified.

The observation of the Single Judge of the High Court that if the submissions made on behalf of the Appellants herein were to be accepted, the mechanism of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder would come to a grinding halt, is not acceptable to us, since the same could lead to a pick and choose method to suit the prosecution.

However, in any event, the percentage of Carbofuran detected in the sample of Pepsico which was sent for examination to the Forensic Laboratory is within the tolerance limits prescribed for Sweetened Carbonated Water with effect from 17th June, 2009.

35. The High Court also misconstrued the provisions of Section 23(1-A)(ee) and (hh) in holding that the same were basically enabling provisions and were not mandatory and could, in any event, be solved by the Central Government by framing Rules thereunder, by which specified tests to be held in designated Laboratories could be spelt out.
Consequently, the High Court also erred in holding that the non-formulation of Rules under the aforesaid provisions of the 1954 Act could not be said to be fatal for the prosecution.

36. As far as Grounds 3, 4 and 5 are concerned, the High  Court failed to consider the reasons given on behalf of the Appellants for not sending the Company's sample to the Forensic Laboratory, to the effect that, since neither any validated method of analysis had been prescribed under Section 23(1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the 1954 Act, nor had any Laboratory been particularly specified for such examination, such an exercise would have been futile.

In our view, no useful purpose could have been served by sending the second sample to the Forensic Laboratory, unless a defined tolerance limit of the presence of the pesticides was available in regard to Sweetened Carbonated Water.

It may be noted that the High Court had itself observed that mere presence of insecticide residue to any extent could not justify an allegation that the article of food was adulterated, but contrary to such observation, the High Court went on to hold that the Sweetened Carbonated Water manufactured by the Appellants was adulterated within the meaning of Section 2(ia)
(h) of the 1954 Act."

18. The ratio of Pepsico India (supra) was followed in R. Gopalakrishnan Vs. Food Inspector, Crl.
Rev. No. 671/200 dated 17.07.2013 by Hon'ble Kerala High Court and it was observed that the observations made in Pepsico India (supra) were not limited to the subject matter of the appeal Da vs Jagjit Singh on 20 August, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/109557362/
8 before the Hon'ble Apex Court in the said case but a general preposition of law was laid down.

sentences.text: It was held that even in case where there is analysis by CFL, the prosecution could not be sustained since the methods of analysis have not been defined under section 23(1A) (hh) of PFA and the laboratories have not been designated for that purpose.

Against the said judgment of Hon'ble Kerala High Court,
criminal appeal bearing No. 2476/2014 was preferred, which was also dismissed.

Relying upon the judgment of Pepsico India (supra), Hon'ble Kerala High Court in Sanjay Parmanand (supra) held as under:
"6.

In this case, admittedly, the laboratory for the analysis of food item was not defined and no validated method of analysis of the food item was specified as mandated under Section 23 (1-A) (ee) and (hh) of the P.F.A. Act.
Therefore, Ext. P21 certificate of analysis cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased in this case was adulterated in view of the decision of the Apex court in Pepsico India Holdings.
(supra).

It was held by the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) that since the Laboratories were not notified and the tests conducted by such laboratories were not admissible in evidence, no prosecution could be based on such report and the accused was entitled to get acquittal.

In the decision of this Court in Gopalakrishnan v. Food Inspector [2013 (3) KLT 455], the court relied on the decision of the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) and found that the Public Analyst's report was not admissible in evidence and accordingly, the Court acquitted the accused.
The matter was referred to a Division Bench and the Division Bench also affirmed the said decision, submitted by the learned counsel for the petitioners and the learned Public Prosecutor.

Even otherwise, in view of the decision in Pepsico India Holdings (supra), the conviction in this case cannot be sustained as no laboratory was notified and no validated method of analysis was specified as mandated under Section 23 (1-A) (ee) and (hh) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954."
19. Hon'ble Bombay High Court in M/s Nestle India Ltd. Vs. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India & Ors., 2015 2 FAC 56

sentences.text: ..........Upon conjoint reading of both these sections quoted hereinabove, it is clear that under section 3(p), "food laboratory" is a laboratory which is either State or Central laboratory or any other allied laboratory which is accredited and recognized by NABL and by the Food Authority under section 43 of the Act.

The laboratory,
therefore, has to pass twin test before it can be said to be a recognized laboratory viz (i) it has to be accredited by NABL and over and above that (ii) it has also to be recognized by the Food Authority under section 43 of the Act.
Sub-section (1) of section 43 makes it abundantly clear that only in that laboratory which is recognized by the Food Authority by Notification, food can be sent for analysis by the Food Analyst.

Upon conjoint reading of the said two provisions, it is clear that the submission made by Mr. Khambata, the learned Senior Counsel for Respondent Nos.
3 and 4 is without any substance.
Section 43(1) mandates that the Food Analyst WPL/1688/2015 has to analyse the food in a laboratory accredited by NABL and also recognized by the Food Authority and notified by it.

It is apparent that therefore if there is non- compliance of the said provisions and if the food is tested in a laboratory which does not fall within the definition of section 3(p) and not recognized by the Food Authority, the analysis made in such laboratory cannot be relied upon.
The Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings Private Limited vs. Food Inspector and Another1 has observed that the provisions are under section mandatory.

sentences.text: The Apex Court in this case held that provisions 23(1-A)(ee) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 for testing the food samples/adulteration are mandatory and not directory.

Though the said observation is made in respect of provisions of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (which has now been repealed by FSS Act,
2006), even under the new Act, the provisions of section 43(1) will have to be held mandatory and not directory.
This is more so when Section 43(1) is read with the definition of the words "food laboratory" in Section 3(p) of the FSS Act, 2006.

The Apex Court in Pepsico India Holding Private Limited (supra) has observed in para 44 as under:-
"44.

The High Court also misconstrued the provisions of Sections 23(1-A)(ee) and (hh) in holding that the same were basically enabling provisions and were 1 (2011) 1 SCC 176 WPL/1688/2015 not mandatory and could, in any event, be solved by the Central Government by framing the Rules thereunder, by which specified tests to be held in designated laboratories could be spelt out.
Consequently, the High Court also erred in holding that the non formulation of rules under the aforesaid provisions of the 1954 Act could not be said to be fatal for the prosecution."

94. Further, if the provisions of sections 43 and 47 are considered, it can be seen that notified laboratories which are referred to in section 47(5) for analysing imported food are laboratories which are separately notified for testing imported food articles as can be seen from the Food Safety and Standards (Laboratory and Samples Analysis) Regulations, 2011.

The contention of Mr.
Khambatta, the learned Senior Counsel appearing on behalf of Respondent Nos. 3 and 4 that only imported food could be tested in the notified laboratories therefore cannot be accepted...

Da vs Jagjit Singh on 20 August, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/109557362/
10 xxxx 95.

Similarly, so far as the food which is manufactured in India is concerned though it is not mentioned that it has to be tested in a notified laboratory, in view of definition of section 3(p) and more particularly the mandate given in section 43(1), the Food Analyst has to analyse the food only in such laboratory which is defined under section 3(p) and recognized by the Food Authority under section 43(1) of the Act."

21. From the above, it appears that the provisions of section 23(1A)(ee) and (hh) of PFA which provide for designation of the laboratories and method of analysis are considered mandatory and the analysis of sample of food where no method of analysis were provided and laboratories were specified, cannot be accepted for launching prosecution under the PFA Act.
It was categorically held in Pepsico India (supra) that the provisions of section 23(1A)(hh) was not an enabling provision but a mandatory one and could be resolved by the Central Govt.

by framing rules specifying the tests to be conducted in designated laboratories and in the absence of such designated laboratories and specified tests, the prosecution could be left to pick and choose a method to suit itself, which cannot be permitted.
22. In view of the above discussion, the accused Jagjit Singh is acquitted of the charges under section 2(ia)(a)(b)&(m) read with Section 16 (1)(a) read with section 7 of the PFA Act.

opennyai_summary.facts:
1. This is a complaint instituted under Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (hereinafter referred to as 'PFA Act') for violation of section 2(ia)(a)(b)(m) and section 7 punishable under section 16 of PFA Act.
It is alleged that he has violated the provisions of Section 7 of the PFA Act, 1954 read with Section 2(ia) (a), (b) & (m) of PFA Act, 1954 which is punishable under section 16(1)(a) of the PFA Act, 1954.
Upon service of summons, appearance was entered by accused and after complying with the provision under section 207 Cr.P.C, vide order dated 09.06.2011, notice for the offences under section 2(ia)(a)(b)&(m) punishable under section 16(1)(a) read with section 7 of PFA Act was served upon the accused to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
However, Ld. Sessions Court, vide its judgment dated 29.03.2023, reversed the judgment in appeal on the ground that key evidences were not put to the accused while recording his statement under section 313 Cr.P.C and the case was remanded back to this court for recording the statement of the accused under section 313 Cr.P.C afresh.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
That the sample of this case was of proprietary food.
And standard of proprietary food has not been defined in the PFA Act, 1954.
The proprietary food has been defined under Rule 37A of Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955 (hereinafter referred to as 'PFA Rules') to be one which is not standardized under the PFA Rules.
The fact that the Public Analyst has admitted that ingredients were mentioned on the Form VII by the Food Inspector raises suspicion on the report of the Public Analyst.
The Hon'ble Apex Court while deciding the case, formulated the following questions for consideration:
"(1) In the absence of any prescribed and validated method of analysis under Section 23(1-A)(hh) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, hereinafter referred to as "the 1954 Act", could a prosecution have been launched against the Appellants based on a report submitted by the Public Analyst using the method of the Directorate General of Health Services (D.G.H.S.)?
(2) Could a prosecution have been launched against the Appellants in the absence of any validated method of analysis to ascertain the percentage of pesticide residue present in a Carbonated beverage, which renders the report of the Public Analyst unreliable, particularly when it does not indicate that such percentage of the pesticide residue is injurious to health and, therefore, adulterated within the meaning of Section 2(ia)
(h) of the aforesaid Act?
(3) What is the effect of non-specification of the level of tolerance in respect of the presence of pesticide residue in Sweetened Carbonated Water in the Table appended to Rule 65(2) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955, hereinafter referred to as "the 1955 Rules"? and (4) What is the liability of the Directors of a company which is said to have committed defaults within the meaning of Section 17 of the 1954 Act, in the light of the decision of this Court in S.M.S. Pharmaceuticals Ltd. Vs. Neeta Bhalla & Anr. [2005 (8) sec 89], when they were neither in charge of nor responsible Da vs Jagjit Singh on 20 August, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/109557362/
7 for the conduct of the business of the Company?"
As far as Grounds 1 and 2 are concerned, the High Court was not convinced with the submission made on behalf of the appellants that in the absence of any prescribed and validated method of analysis under Section 23(1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the 1954 Act,
the report of the Public Analyst, who had used the DGHS method, could not be relied upon, especially when even the Laboratories, where the test for detection of insecticides and pesticides in an article of food could be undertaken, had not been specified.
35. The High Court also misconstrued the provisions of Section 23(1-A)(ee) and (hh) in holding that the same were basically enabling provisions and were not mandatory and could, in any event, be solved by the Central Government by framing Rules thereunder, by which specified tests to be held in designated Laboratories could be spelt out.
Consequently, the High Court also erred in holding that the non-formulation of Rules under the aforesaid provisions of the 1954 Act could not be said to be fatal for the prosecution.
36. As far as Grounds 3, 4 and 5 are concerned, the High  Court failed to consider the reasons given on behalf of the Appellants for not sending the Company's sample to the Forensic Laboratory, to the effect that, since neither any validated method of analysis had been prescribed under Section 23(1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the 1954 Act, nor had any Laboratory been particularly specified for such examination, such an exercise would have been futile.
In our view, no useful purpose could have been served by sending the second sample to the Forensic Laboratory, unless a defined tolerance limit of the presence of the pesticides was available in regard to Sweetened Carbonated Water.
Similar view was again taken in Mohanan P. & Ors. Vs. State of Kerala & Anr., 2022 1 FAC 322 by Hon'ble Kerala High Court.
The laboratory,
therefore, has to pass twin test before it can be said to be a recognized laboratory viz (i) it has to be accredited by NABL and over and above that (ii) it has also to be recognized by the Food Authority under section 43 of the Act.
Sub-section (1) of section 43 makes it abundantly clear that only in that laboratory which is recognized by the Food Authority by Notification, food can be sent for analysis by the Food Analyst.
Section 43(1) mandates that the Food Analyst WPL/1688/2015 has to analyse the food in a laboratory accredited by NABL and also recognized by the Food Authority and notified by it.
It is apparent that therefore if there is non- compliance of the said provisions and if the food is tested in a laboratory which does not fall within the definition of section 3(p) and not recognized by the Food Authority, the analysis made in such laboratory cannot be relied upon.
The Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings Private Limited vs. Food Inspector and Another1 has observed that the provisions are under section mandatory.
94. Further, if the provisions of sections 43 and 47 are considered, it can be seen that notified laboratories which are referred to in section 47(5) for analysing imported food are laboratories which are separately notified for testing imported food articles as can be seen from the Food Safety and Standards (Laboratory and Samples Analysis) Regulations, 2011.
21. From the above, it appears that the provisions of section 23(1A)(ee) and (hh) of PFA which provide for designation of the laboratories and method of analysis are considered mandatory and the analysis of sample of food where no method of analysis were provided and laboratories were specified, cannot be accepted for launching prosecution under the PFA Act.
It was categorically held in Pepsico India (supra) that the provisions of section 23(1A)(hh) was not an enabling provision but a mandatory one and could be resolved by the Central Govt.
by framing rules specifying the tests to be conducted in designated laboratories and in the absence of such designated laboratories and specified tests, the prosecution could be left to pick and choose a method to suit itself, which cannot be permitted.
